goal: The reader is a person or an AI who reads the document for a purpose, at any time after its writer writes it. They read it in its own language or through a machine translation into theirs. The reader reads once from the top and only the parts their purpose needs, and takes in what the document says as its writer meant.

necessary_conditions.what: Does the reader find each fact said in one place only, in the document or in what they read beside it, with every other place pointing there, so that two places never tell them different things?
Coming to the document for a purpose, can the reader tell from each heading and the sentence under it what the section gives them, so they read the sections their purpose needs and skip the rest?

Where the document gives steps in order, choices that depend on a case, or how several things relate, does the reader see it at a glance, without piecing it together from sentences, so that they grasp it without effort?

Reading from the top, can the reader understand each sentence from what they have read before it, without turning back, reading ahead, or knowing what the document neither says nor points to, so that they read straight through?
When the reader reads any sentence once, as written or through a machine translation into their own language, can they say who or what does what in it, so that no sentence is misread?
Each time the reader meets a name, can they tell rightly whether it names a thing they have already met, and which one, so that they never take two things for one or one thing for two?
When the reader meets a word they haven't used themselves, can they tell what it means right where they meet it, so that no word stops them?
Does each word the reader reads carry part of what the document says, so that no word costs them time and gives them nothing?

practices.thinking: The document says each fact, including one that a figure draws or the work itself shows, in the one place where the reader looks for it. Every other place points there. A change made in that one place then reaches every reader, as a [single source of truth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_source_of_truth) does.

steps.text: Where two places say a fact in different ways, keep both, and send the difference back so that someone settles it with what the document says. Choosing one would change what the document says.
Replace each other place's copy with a link to that place, saying in a few words what the reader finds there.

practices.thinking: The reader picks sections by their headings and first sentences. So each section holds one thing and says at its start what it gives, as readers scan the first words of [headings](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/headings-pickup-lines/).

steps.text: Start each heading with the words that tell the most.

Name the reader and the purposes they come with. Read only the headings and first sentences for each purpose. Where the reader would miss a section that the purpose needs, or read one that it doesn't need, rewrite the section's heading or first sentence.

practices.thinking: The reader grasps at once an order or a relation that the form of a list, a table, or a diagram shows. When sentences tell the same, the reader must piece it together.

steps.text: Choose a form whose shape shows that order or relation, such as a numbered list for steps in order, a bulleted list for items whose order doesn't matter, a table for things compared on the same points, or a diagram for who passes what to whom.
Draw a sequence diagram as text that the page draws, such as Mermaid inside the document, as its steps go from top to bottom and leave no layout to choose.

Draw a diagram of structure, such as parts and what passes between them, as a drawing whose layout the writer sets, such as an SVG file beside the document shown as an image, as its layout carries its meaning.
Write in each box only its part's name, and at most its type, and what each part does in a list under the figure, by the part's name, as a box that holds sentences hides the layout it stands in.

Draw every part alike in shape and color, and set one apart only where the reader must tell it apart and its name and type don't, as a shape such as a database's cylinder says what the part may not be, and a color draws the eye to a part that needs no more weight than the rest.

Lay the parts out so that the layout shows the reader something before they read a line: parts that belong together side by side in a frame that names what holds them together, the groups in the order the reader meets them, such as from the top left along the course a run takes, and the part most others join in the middle. Boxes set in a grid tell nothing, and the reader must trace every line.

Draw a table the reader takes in whole at a glance, such as which tests cover which part, as an SVG in the same way, so its marks and groups line up. Keep a table the reader looks a row up in as Markdown, so they can search and copy it.
Set the SVG's colors under prefers-color-scheme, so that it follows the page's light or dark scheme.

practices.thinking: Each sentence comes after everything it rests on, so the reader never holds a sentence open while they look for what it needs.

steps.text: Where a sentence rests on something outside the document, such as an earlier talk, say it in the sentence or link to the place that says it.
Start each sentence with what the reader already has, and end it with what's new, the given-new order of [information structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_structure).

Put a rule's conditions and exceptions beside the rule, where the reader takes them in most easily. Put a short condition before its instruction, so that a reader whose case it isn't can skip the instruction.

practices.thinking: A sentence that makes one point, names who acts, and keeps plain order has one reading for the reader and for a machine translator alike, as [Simplified Technical English](https://www.asd-ste100.org) and the [Google developer documentation style guide](https://developers.google.com/style/voice) write.

steps.text: Split a sentence that makes more than one point, or that links more than two clauses with "and," "or," or "but," into one sentence for each point.
Follow the subject at once with an active verb that carries the action. Keep the object close after the verb. Turn a noun made from a verb back into the verb.
Keep the small words that show the structure of a sentence, such as articles, "that," "who," "then," and "of."
Where a pronoun or a "which" could point to two nouns, replace it with the noun it means. Break a string of nouns apart with prepositions.
Read each sentence once as a machine translator would, word by word in its order and with nothing from outside it, and say who does what. Where the sentence reads two ways, reword it.

practices.thinking: Each thing has one name, the one its reader already uses, written the same way each time. Each name names one thing. The reader, and a translator, then keep one picture of each thing from start to end.

The reader takes each word with the meaning they already give it. So the writer replaces a word new to the reader with everyday words, even a word the writer's team uses every day, or gives its meaning where the reader first meets it.

steps.text: Write each abbreviation out in full where the reader first meets it, as the [Google developer documentation style guide](https://developers.google.com/style/abbreviations) does.
Where the document gives a common word a meaning of its own, replace it with a word the reader doesn't already read another way.

practices.thinking: A word or a sentence that carries nothing of what the document says still costs the reader time, so it goes. A word that shows the structure of a sentence stays.

steps.text: Read each changed section again from the top, and check that it still says all it said before.
